listen_text: Chapter. Semantics. Editorial note. This chapter collects definitions for semantics for intuitionistic logic. So far only Kripke and topological semantics are covered. There are no examples yet, either of how models make formulas true or of proofs that formulas are valid. End editorial note.

Section. Introduction. No logic is satisfactorily described without a semantics, and intuitionistic logic is no exception. Whereas for classical logic, the semantics based on valuations is canonical, there are several competing semantics for intuitionistic logic. None of them are completely satisfactory in the sense that they give an intuitionistically acceptable account of the meanings of the connectives. The semantics based on relational models, similar to the semantics for modal logics, is perhaps the most popular one. In this semantics, propositional variables are assigned to worlds, and these worlds are related by an accessibility relation. That relation is always a partial order, that is, it is reflexive, antisymmetric, and transitive. Intuitively, you might think of these worlds as states of knowledge or “evidentiary situations.” A state w prime is accessible from w if and only if, for all we know, w prime is a possible (future) state of knowledge, that is, one that is compatible with what's known at w . Once a proposition is known, it can't become un-known, that is, whenever A is known at w and world w prime is accessible from world w , A is known at w prime as well. So “knowledge” is monotonic with respect to the accessibility relation. If we define “ A is known” as in epistemic logic as “true in all epistemic alternatives,” then A and B is known at w if in all epistemic alternatives, both A and B are known. But since knowledge is monotonic and R is reflexive, that means that A and B is known at w if and only if A and B are known at w . For the same reason, A or B is known at w if and only if at least one of them is known. So for conjunction and disjunction , the truth conditions of the connectives coincide with those in classical logic. The truth conditions for the conditional, however, differ from classical logic. if A, then B is known at w if and only if at no w prime with world w prime is accessible from world w , A is known without B also being known. This is not the same as the condition that A is unknown or B is known at w . For if we know neither A nor B at w , there might be a future epistemic state w prime with world w prime is accessible from world w such that at w prime , A is known without also coming to know B . We know not A only if there is no possible future epistemic state in which we know A . Here the idea is that if A were knowable, then in some possible future epistemic state A becomes known. Since we can't know falsity , in that future epistemic state, we would know A but not know falsity . On this interpretation the principle of excluded middle fails. For there are some A which we don't yet know, but which we might come to know. For such a formula A , both A and not A are unknown, so A or not A is not known. But we do know, for example, that not both A and not A . For no future state in which we know both A and not A is possible, and we know this independently of whether or not we know A or not A . Relational models are not the only available semantics for intuitionistic logic. The topological semantics is another: here propositions are interpreted as open sets in a topological space, and the connectives are interpreted as operations on these sets (for example, conjunction corresponds to intersection). End section.

In order to give a precise semantics for intuitionistic propositional logic, we have to give a definition of what counts as a model relative to which we can evaluate formulas. On the basis of such a definition it is then also possible to define semantics notions such as validity and entailment. One such semantics is given by relational models. Definition. A relational model for intuitionistic propositional logic is a triple model M is the ordered triple W, R, V , where List. Next item. W is a non-empty set, Next item. R is a partial order (that is, a reflexive, antisymmetric, and transitive binary relation) on W , and Next item. V is a function assigning to each propositional variable p a subset of W , such that Next item. V is monotone with respect to R , that is, if w belongs to V of p and world w prime is accessible from world w , then w prime belongs to V of p . End list. End definition. Definition. Next item. Next item. End list. We write model M does not satisfy A at world w if not model M satisfies A at world w . This exercise remains unsolved. Proposition. Truth at worlds is monotonic with respect to R , that is, if model M satisfies A at world w and world w prime is accessible from world w , then model M satisfies A at world w prime . End proposition. listen_text: Section. Topological Semantics. Another way to provide a semantics for intuitionistic logic is using the mathematical concept of a topology. Definition. Let X be a set. A topology on X is a set script O is a subset of the power set of X that satisfies the properties below. The elements of script O are called the open sets of the topology. The set X together with script O is called a topological space. List. Next item. The empty set and the entire space are open: the empty set , X belongs to script O . Next item. Open sets are closed under finite intersections: if U , V belongs to script O then the intersection of U and V belongs to script O Next item. Open sets are closed under arbitrary unions: if U subscript i belongs to script O for all i belongs to I , then the union of all U subscript i such that i belongs to I, belongs to script O . End list. End definition. We may write X for a topology if the collection of open sets can be inferred from the context; note that, still, only after X is endowed with open sets can it be called a topology. Definition. A topological model of intuitionistic propositional logic is a triple topological model X is the ordered triple X, script O, V where script O is a topology on X and V is a function assigning an open set in script O to each propositional variable. Given a topological model topological model X , we can define the open-set proposition for A in X inductively as follows: List. Next item. the open-set proposition for falsity in X equals the empty set Next item. the open-set proposition for p in X equals V of p Next item. the proposition for A and B in X equals the intersection of the proposition for A and the proposition for B Next item. the proposition for A or B in X equals the union of the proposition for A and the proposition for B Next item. the proposition for if A then B in X equals the interior of the union of X minus the proposition for A and the proposition for B End list. Here, the interior of V is the function that maps a set V is a subset of X to its interior, that is, the union of all open sets it contains. In other words, Displayed expression. the interior of V equals the union of all U such that U is a subset of V and U belongs to script O. End displayed expression. End definition. Note that the interior of any set is always open, since it is a union of open sets. Thus, the open-set proposition for A in X is always an open set. Although topological semantics is highly abstract, there are ways to think about it that might motivate it. Suppose that the elements, or “points,” of X are points at which statements can be evaluated. The set of all points where A is true is the proposition expressed by A . Not every set of points is a potential proposition; only the elements of script O are. A entails B if and only if B is true at every point at which A is true, that is, the proposition for A in X is a subset of the proposition for B in X , for all X . The absurd statement falsity is never true, so the open-set proposition for falsity in X equals the empty set . How must the propositions expressed by B and C , B or C , and if B, then C be related to those expressed by B and C for the intuitionistically valid laws to hold, that is, so that B is derivable from A if and only if the proposition for A in X is a proper subset of the proposition for B in X ? We require A is derivable from falsity for any A , which is satisfied because the empty set is a subset of U for all U . Since B is derivable from B and C , we require that the proposition for B and C is a subset of the proposition for B , and similarly the proposition for B and C is a subset of the proposition for C . The largest set satisfying W is a subset of U and W is a subset of V is the intersection of U and V . Conversely, B or C is derivable from B and B or C is derivable from C , and so we require that the proposition for B is a subset of the proposition for B or C and the proposition for C is a subset of the proposition for B or C . The smallest set W such that U is a subset of W and V is a subset of W is the union of U and V . The definition for conditional is tricky: if A, then B expresses the weakest proposition that, combined with A , entails B . That if A, then B combined with A entails B is clear from B is derivable from the conditional from A to B together with A . So the proposition for if A then B in X should be the greatest open set such that the intersection of the proposition for if A then B and the proposition for A is a proper subset of the proposition for B , leading to our definition.
